Question 4 [12 marks]: Evaluate the effect of the Nazi regime on cultural expression in Germany. Integrate evidence from Sources C and D to support your answer.

MARKING CRITERIA (out of 12):
10–12 marks: Provides a comprehensive evaluation of the impact of the Nazi regime on cultural expression in Germany | Effectively integrates evidence from Source C and D to support response | Presents a well-structured, logical and cohesive response using appropriate historical terms and concepts
7–9 marks: Provides an evaluation of the impact of the Nazi regime on cultural expression in Germany | Integrates evidence from Source C and D to support response | Presents a structured response using appropriate historical terms and concepts
4–6 marks: Describes the impact of the Nazi regime on cultural expression in Germany | Makes some reference to Source C and/or D | Communicates using some historical terms and concepts
1–3 marks: Makes a general statement(s) in relation to the question | May use some historical terms and/or concepts


ANSWERS COULD INCLUDE (the student does not need every point):
Possible thesis:
The Reich Chamber of Culture effectively transformed most cultural expression in Germany so that it aligned with Nazi ideology; however, it could not fully supress all forms of artistic dissent.
OR The Nazis were very effective in controlling cultural expression in Germany. They produced a range of propagandistic films and art and ensured that most other works that were introduced were aligned with Nazi ideology.
Art
• Degenerate Art exhibition (1938) condemned modernist styles like Expressionism and Cubism (Source C). However, despite the intention of the exhibition, many secretly used this as an opportunity to admire the artwork.
• Artists like Otto Dix and Ernst Ludwig Kirchner were banned; Nazi art promoted Aryan ideals.
Architecture
• Albert Speer’s neoclassical designs emphasised Nazi power (eg the Reich Chancellery)
• Bauhaus was shut down in 1933 for being too ‘internationalist’.
Music
• Jazz and Swing were banned as they were considered ‘degenerate’ (Source D)
• Wagner and Beethoven were promoted; Schoenberg’s avant-garde music was suppressed.
Radio and propaganda
• The Volksempfänger (‘Peoples Receiver’ or Nazi radio) made Nazi broadcasts widely accessible
• Music and programs reinforced nationalism, banning foreign influences.
Film
• Leni Riefenstahl’s ‘Triumph of the Will’ (1935) glorified Hitler and Nazi power
• Films were used for propaganda, reinforcing nationalism and militarism.
